Should books, music, movies, magazines, and other reading materials be removed from shelves if they are found to be offensive? I strongly believe that this is not a good idea. As the author Katherine Paterson aptly stated, if we remove books from shelves, it results in "no more books for any of us to read." This rings true because there are many books that some individuals may find offensive, but such readers may not understand the materials that they read.

One reason why censorship of reading materials is unfavorable is that America is a country that values freedom of speech and expression. We have the right to speak and write about whatever we desire. It is unfair to take away a writer's material just because a reader finds the topic offensive. Doing so is akin to putting duct tape on the writer's mouth. If we give readers the right to express what is on their minds, then writers should have the same privilege. Removing a book or other materials is equivalent to censoring the writer's thoughts.

Another reason why censorship of reading materials is not advisable is that reading is an essential part of acquiring knowledge. When we read, we learn new things that we may not have known before. It could be a new event, an unfamiliar place, the significance of good grammar, the different styles of writing, or knowledge about a particular subject. Reading is an entertaining way of learning new things, and it plays a crucial role in our lives.

Moreover, reading can also help readers know that they are not alone in their struggles or life situations. For instance, reading a story about a particular issue like a break-up, a loss, or a family problem can help readers know that someone else has been down that road, and they will not feel alone. Taking away such literature from the library shelf robs readers of that shared experience, which could provide comfort to a person in distress.

Finally, censoring reading materials may not work because the topic may still exist elsewhere. Even if you delete books, music, movies or magazines from library shelves, the same topic can be found on other media sources, like social media platforms or other organizations. Additionally, people will continue to discuss the topic even if it's been removed from the library's shelves. It's like locking a bird in a cage but not allowing it to fly away or telling a cat or dog not to escape, but they would try to do so. Removing materials will not eliminate the subject entirely.

In summary, while reading materials may offend some readers, it is not in the best interest of anyone to censor them. It is better to ignore it and move on. If someone does not like the topic of a particular material, others would, and that's always good to think about. Perhaps the reader simply does not understand the subject, and reading about it will give them a chance to understand it and maybe even appreciate it. Books, music, movies, magazines are out there to teach us something new, so it is better to keep an open mind and learn.

Sincerely,

As Katherine Paterson, the author of Bridge to Terabithia, wisely said, "If I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else. And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us." Censorship in libraries is a hotly debated topic, with some people advocating for certain books, music, movies, and magazines to be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive. However, I firmly believe that no reading material should be taken off the shelf, and every book has the potential to help a child learn and grow.

Removing books from libraries can limit a child's exposure to different experiences and perspectives. Every person is unique, with their own interests and preferences, and libraries should provide a wide range of reading options for everyone to explore. When we limit the themes and topics of books in our libraries, we risk discouraging children from reading altogether. Every book has a different plot and a different moral, and removing them from the shelves takes away the chance for a child to learn important life lessons.

Furthermore, censorship in libraries can have the unintended consequence of sheltering children from reality. Certain books may touch on sensitive or controversial topics, but avoiding them won't change the fact that these topics exist in the world. It's important for children to learn about and grapple with complex issues through literature, under the guidance of their guardians. In that way, they can develop critical thinking skills and learn how to form their own opinions.

Ultimately, the decision to read a certain book should rest with the child's guardian. If a parent or guardian believes that a particular book is not suitable for their child, they can choose to forbid their child from reading it. It's not up to the library to determine what is offensive or bad for everyone – these are subjective opinions that vary from person to person.

In conclusion, censorship in libraries is unnecessary and can limit a child's education and growth. Everyone enjoys different kinds of books, and leaving options open for students is the best way to encourage reading. Each book tells a different story and teaches a different moral, and every child deserves the chance to read any book they want, unless their guardian forbids it. Let's keep the shelves open and give children the opportunity to explore and learn from the stories they choose.
